plateosaurus.notes: Plateosaurus small skull contained plump plant-crushing teeth. Its long mobile neck and short, muscular forelimbs allowed it to eat taller plants and trees, thus giving it an evolutionary advantage. It grasped vegetation with its hands, and may have used its sharp claws for defense. A bipedal (two-legged) dinosaur, Plateosaurus stood on powerful hind limbs, yet walked on its toes. If this dinosaur looks familiar to the larger Brachiosaurus and other sauropods that you have seen before that is because Plateosaurus is a prosauropod, or an ancient relative of the massive longnecked creatures that roamed the earth in the Jurassic Period.

allosaurus.attributes: The first giant predatory dinosaur in USA
allosaurus.notes: Allosaurus name means different lizard because of its concave vertebrae that were unique at the time of its formal naming in 1877 in Colorado. Its early discovery amidst the “Bone Wars,” a competitive period of fossil hunting in the late 1800s, meant that a significant number of Allosaurus fossils were uncovered quickly, making it one of the first well-known theropods and the stuff of legend for years to come. With a large but light skull and dozens of razor sharp, serrated teeth, Allosaurus, was built to feed on smaller dinosaurs in its habitat. It had short strong forelimbs with three-fingers, unlike five-fingered dinosaurs that had come earlier) and powerful hindlimbs that allowed it to charge into any situation while being balanced by its impressive tail. Allosaurus was at the top of its food chain and one of the largest most dominant theropods of the Jurassic Period.

kentrosaurus.notes: Kentrosaurus was a small stegosaurian dinosaur with dramatic spikes along its back and tail. Its tail was its primary type of defense and could cover a 180-degree arc at speeds exceeding 50 km/h! An Herbivore that lived alongside larger sauropods and had to defend itself from Allosuaurs, Kentrosaurus habitat in Tanzania is an excellent example of the shift in tectonic plates that spread dinosaurs all over the world. A semi-detached section of Africa, Kentrosaurus shares the same common ancestors as larger Stegosaurus but developed on a separate part of the Earth with distinct feaures that helped it survive along the coasts of Africa.

yinlong.attributes: The oldest and most primitive ceratopsian
yinlong.notes: A very recent addition to the ever-developing story of dinosaurs, Yinlong was named in 2006 by a coalition of American and Chinese scientists. Its name means “hidden dragon” which provides further insight into the magic of dinosaurs and scientists’ sense of humor. Long, which means “dragon” is the most common reference to dinosaurs in China because when dinosaur bones were first discovered in Asia they were thought to be the remains of ancient dragons. In fact, Chineselore still holds that the nation is descended from dragons. The full meaning for Yinlong is “hidden dragon,” which is a direct reference to the film Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon, because major segments of the movie were filmed in the region where the dinosaur was discovered. A small but highly instructive dinosaur, Yinlong is a ceratopsian, deriving from the same family as the well known Triceratops. Despite having no visible horns, its skull’s deep, wide shape marks it as belonging to this suborder.

hesperosaurus.attributes: Back plates from front to rear
hesperosaurus.notes: Hesperosaurus is a Herbivore dinosaurs that also hails from the stegosaurian clan. Its flexible dual-plated armor on its back and spiked tail are very similar to the well-known Stegosaurus. Not uncovered until 1985 and not named until 2001, Hesperosaurus is another relatively new addition to the dinosaur story, and adds a new chapter to it. Hesperosaurus is, in fact the oldest known stegosaur known to science – an earlier, squattier, and longer ancestor of Stegosaurus. This recent discovery provides additional insight into the vastness of time associated with each of the Periods in which dinosaurs lived. Stegosaurus lived from 155 to 150 million years ago and Hesperosaurus lived 156 million years ago. It might seem that the two species just missed each other when they actually lived one million years apart! For comparison, the entirety of human history since homo sapiens first appeared is “only” 300,000 years long.

saurophaganax.notes: Saurophaganax was big! In fact, it was one of the largest carnivores of the entire Jurassic Period. An Allosaur at the very top of the food chain, Saurophaganax was also very rare It is found in less than one percent (1%) of the Allosaurs discovered in the Morrison Formation – a rich deposit of dinosaur fossils in the Western United States and Canada that stretches from Saskatchewan to New Mexico.
saurophaganax.meaning: « The king who feeds on lizards »

tyrannosaurusrextrex.notes: With an enormous skull filled with up to sixty, 15 cm serrated teeth Tyranosaurus rex could generate bite forces as great as 240 MPa. This was one of the largest dinosaurs and largest Carnivores ever, and it could easily bite through both flesh and bone. Tyrannosaurus most likely traveled in herds and hunted duck- billed dinosaurs, horned dinosaurs, and, even one another. A surprising fact: A recent study revealed that T. rex only lived to age 30!

carnotaurus.attributes: Small arms and horns on its head
carnotaurus.notes: A truly distinctive theropod, Carnotaurus had thick horns above the eyes, and a very deep skull sitting on a muscular neck. In addition to its fear inspiring features, Carnotaurus was also built for speed: a light skeleton and powerful hindlimbs allowed it to pursue its prey at speeds of up to 65 Km/h! Carnotaurus appeared to hunt smaller prey as well as larger sauropods. Picture the fear coming over a slow moving sauropod when it saw this “bull” of a dinosaur charging at it at full speed!

triceratopstriceratops.notes: A member of the Ceratopsidae family of dinosaurs, Triceratops was one of the last dinosaurs on Earth, and lived right up until the extinction of all dinosaurs. Its large head, adorned with neck frills and three horns, could grow to be over 2,5 m long. Triceratops were very successful in the Cretaceous Period – hundreds of specimens have been unearthed across its range over North America – and it was one of the last of the Ceratopsidae (there were more than 30 “horned face” species of dinosaur to walk the Earth). Early researchers first thought Triceratops fossils were the remains of a giant bison. Triceratops appear to have used their horns mostly for courtship displays, however the discovery of large puncture wounds indicate that they also defended their territory against other large Herbivores using their powerful heads. Living in the same biosphere as Tyrannosaurus rex, Triceratops were hunted by them and had to use their incredible size and weight to deter such fatal encounters.

ankylosaurus.attributes: Massive knobs and plates of bone
ankylosaurus.notes: Ankylosaurus was armored to the extreme! Huge plates of bone in its back, fused bones in its skull and its club-like tail allowed this massive, tank-like Herbivore to mostly graze peacefully. It fed using small, leaf-shaped teeth to crush vegetation with an up and down jaw movement but most likely not a grinding movement. Living low to the ground, Ankylosaurus depended on low shrubs and grasses to survive – and they appear to have been primarily solitary individuals, not moving in large herds. The last of the dinosaurs, Ankylosaurus would have witnessed the end of the Cretaceous, and may have used the extra chambers in their nasal cavities to call out one last warning as debris from the meteor that devastated the Earth rained down.

parasaurolophus.attributes: Duck-billed dinosaur with crest on head
parasaurolophus.notes: Parasaurolophus are remarkable for their head adornments that extend their skulls into a curving crown. Inside of this crest are hollow chambers that connected to the nasal cavity. It is thought that these cavities were used as resonance chambers to communicate over long distances with others in large herds to call out for food or in case of danger. Parasaurolophus also had fascinating teeth and jaws. Their heads contain hundreds of teeth, which were constantly being replaced. As a dinosaur that could walk on its hind legs or all fours, Parasaurolophus had a variety of feeding options: they could eat from the ground on or reach up to more than 3 m, and sometimes stored food in cheek-like structures in their mouths as a reserve. A member of the Hadrosauridae family, Parasaurolophus were , also called “duck billed” dinosaurs, a type of dinosaur that had an incredible range. Fossils of duckbilled dinosaurs have been found on every continent including Antarctica!

dimetrodon.notes: Dimetrodon was an apex predator during the last phase of the Paleozoic Era, which came before the Age of Dinosaurs in the Mesozoic Era. Compact and strong,Dimetrodon feasted on fish and reptiles with its many sized teeth in its powerful jaw. Dimetrodon’s most distinguishing feature was its tall back sail formed by long spines connected to its vertebrae. Once thought to control body temperature, the sail was most likely used to attract mates and to deter predators. Although it is often mistaken for a dinosaur, Dimetrodon is actually a closer relative to mammals like us!

pachycephalosaurus.attributes: Dinosaur with a thick, domed head
pachycephalosaurus.notes: Pachycephalosaurus is famous for its large bony skull and domelike crest, which could be up to 25 cm thick. Despite the size of its skull, Pachycephalosaurus brains were relatively small, leading scientists to conclude that this dramatic headpiece was used for display and possibly to head-butt others similar to how big horn sheep do today. The head also featured large, round, forward-facing eye sockets, indicating that Pachycephalosaurus may have had stereo vision, which could have been crucial in head-butting contests!

suchomimus.notes: A relatively recent discovery to the living history of dinosaurs, Suchomimus was named in 1998, and continuous to help our understanding that dinosaurs were larger and wilder looking than we have ever imagined. A spinosaurid dinosaur, Suchomimus mouth with its distinctive kink and pronounced teeth was similar to a crocodiles, which earned it its name meaning “crocodile mimic”. Suchomimus was a huge and strong animal that fed on fish along the shores of Gandwana. Similar spinosaurid dinosaurs, including Baryonyx in the U.K., have been found around the world, indicating that they evolved from a common ancestor when Earth was one large land mass called Pangea.

baryonyx.attributes: Large, heavy claw at the end of its forelimbs
baryonyx.notes: First discovered in Surrey, England in 1983, Baryonyx was an immediate sensation because of where such a sizable theropod was discovered, and because of its very large claw on the first forefinger. Typically, dinosaurs in upper Laurasia (the northern supercontinent after Pangea’s breakup), thought to be smaller in stature because of the abundance of water and limited resources. Baryonyx, however, was thought to be a full fledged carnivorous theropod…until more research was conducted. Further research revealed that, while carnivorous, Baryonyx was also piscivorous (fish-eating), and may have had semi-aquatic habits to sustain itself in the waters around Northern Laurasia. An opportunistic predator, Baryonyx ate what flesh it could find, be it from the sea, larger prey, juvenile Igunanodon, and wounded pterosaurs. It may not seem surprising now when you look at Baryonyx, but it took researchers some time before they classified it as a spinosaurid – a relative of the mighty and fierce Spinosaurus.

velociraptor.attributes: Distinctive sickle claw on the second toe
velociraptor.notes: A small, carnivorous dinosaur from Mongolia, Velociraptor had sharp serrated teeth, sharp, clawed hands and feet, and a stiff bony tail. Swift, and agile because of its unique stance on two toes, it was constantly ready to slash with large retractable claws on its other toes. Velociraptor used its claws to the detriment of anything it hunted; often slicing open the bellies of its victims. Marks in its bones indicate that Velociraptor was covered in feathers, which helps support the connection between dinosaurs and modern birds. If you know the “Jurassic Park” movies, you will be surprised by the slight size of the Velociraptor, but don’t be alarmed: even though they were called Raptors in the films, they were actually modeled after a larger North American relative named Deinonychus.

iguanodon.attributes: Lived in vast herds, with hundreds of thousands of individuals
iguanodon.notes: One of the first dinosaurs to be discovered Iguandon was initially thought to be a giant lizard or perhaps even evidence of real dragons! Iguanodon were often found in herds as they traveled the lands of Laurasia. They moved on all fours but could also stand on their hind legs to feed on higher plants and low trees. When they ate, their teeth came completely together, which was rare among dinosaurs and even in reptiles today. They had a unique hoof formation in the middle of their hands but also had opposable small finger that was used grasp branches in a manner similar to a human thumb. This “thumb” served another purpose as well – it sported a horn- covered spike used for fighting and defense.

dilophosaurus.attributes: Medium size dino with crests on head
dilophosaurus.notes: A carnivorous, bipedal, theropod, Dilophosaurus features a pair of irregularly shaped crowns on its skull that most likely developed to attract mates. With well developed forelimbs that had hands capable of grasping and slashing, Dilophosaurus propelled itself with its hind limbs. Curiously, however, this dinosaur also was known to rest in a bird-like posture, a trait perhaps that has continued to dinosaurs living ancestors: Birds. Made famous by the book and movie Jurassic Park, Dilophosaurus depiction in the story was highly fictionalized by the author Michael Crichton in order to advance the storyline – it did not have a flaring neck frill, nor did it spew deadly toxins to incapacitate its prey. A recent study found that Dilophosaurus had a powerful jaw bone that but its bite force was relatively weak, meaning it was more likely a scavenger than a predatory hunter.

dilophosaurus2.attributes: Medium size dino with crests on head
dilophosaurus2.notes: A carnivorous, bipedal, theropod, Dilophosaurus features a pair of irregularly shaped crowns on its skull that most likely developed to attract mates. With well developed forelimbs that had hands capable of grasping and slashing, Dilophosaurus propelled itself with its hind limbs. Curiously, however, this dinosaur also was known to rest in a bird-like posture, a trait perhaps that has continued to dinosaurs living ancestors: Birds. Made famous by the book and movie Jurassic Park, Dilophosaurus depiction in the story was highly fictionalized by the author Michael Crichton in order to advance the storyline – it did not have a flaring neck frill, nor did it spew deadly toxins to incapacitate its prey. A recent study found that Dilophosaurus had a powerful jaw bone that but its bite force was relatively weak, meaning it was more likely a scavenger than a predatory hunter.

styracosaurus.attributes: Medium size dino with crests on head
styracosaurus.notes: The bulky body of Styracosaurus resembled that of a rhinoceros. It had powerful shoulders which may have been useful in intraspecies combat. Styracosaurus had a relatively short tail. Each toe bore a hooflike ungual which was sheathed in horn. Styracosaurus had a unique dental structure. Their mouths were equipped with a large beak and tooth batteries in the cheeks. Styracosaurus is an amazing animal with a story riddled with confusion and discovery. It may have been a gentle grazer, but it was probably still a formidable force to be reckoned with. Whether its horn and frill were for display or defence, local predators undoubtedly wouldn’t have wanted to come into a head-on confrontation with this prehistoric beast.

pteranodon.attributes: Long crest at the back of the skull
pteranodon.notes: The Pteranodon was a large flying reptile from the now- extinct order of pterosaurs, likely one of the last of its kind before these creatures disappeared at the end of the Cretaceous period around 66 million years ago. It had a long, toothless beak, which suited it for catching fish by skimming the surfaces of seas and oceans, much like a pelican. Often confused with the pterodactyl, which lived about 150 million years ago, the pterodactyl had teeth but lacked the crest seen on the Pteranodon, and its remains have been found in North America and Europe. With an impressive wingspan of 6 to 8 meters, the Pteranodon was only outmatched in size by a few other species of pterosaurs, most notably Quetzalcoatlus northropi, the largest flying creature ever known.

pterodactyl.attributes: Ailes formées par une membrane entre le doigt allongé et les membres postérieurs Wings formed by a cutaneous and muscular membrane extending from its elongated fourth finger to its hind limbs
pterodactyl.notes: Pterodactylus was the first pterosaur to be named and identified as a flying reptile and one of the first prehistoric reptiles to ever be discovered. Pterodactylus was a generalist carnivore that probably fed on a variety of invertebrates and vertebrates. It was a small pterosaur compared to other famous genera such as Pteranodon and Quetzalcoatlus, and it also lived earlier.

aliwalia.notes: Aliwalia’s story fascinates us because it is a case of mistaken identity – as well as an example of how paleontologists are still learning about the ancient past. Initially identified by just two bone fragments, scientists thought Aliwalia was another Herbivore (plant eating) dinosaur named Eucnemesaurus. Further investigation, however, revealed that this massive dinosaur for its time was actually a carnivorous dinosaur and one of the earliest dinosaurs to ever appear! The work of paleontologists (scientists who study the ancient past) never ends, and they are always trying to decipher the mysteries that of the dinosaurs that are embedded in rock across the planet.

morosintrepidus.attributes: L’un des plus petits tyrannosauroïdes connus One of the smallest tyrannosauroids to have ever existed
morosintrepidus.notes: Moros is a genus of small tyrannosauroid theropod dinosaur that lived during the Late Cretaceous period in what is now Utah, represents one of the earliest known diagnostic tyrannosauroid material from North America. Moros was a small-bodied, cursorial tyrannosauroid. The foot bones were extremely slender, with metatarsal proportions found to be more similar to ornithomimids than to other Late Cretaceous tyrannosauroids.

liliensternus.notes: Known as a neotheropod (new theropod) it shares a lineage with the most famous dinosaur of them all, Tyrannosaurus rex!. Liliensternus sported a prominent head crest and could move with great speed. It most likely inhabited floodplains where it used it slashing teeth to attack larger, yet more docile, prosauropods and its speed to catch swifter prey.

melanorosaurus.notes: An Herbivore dinosaur Melanorosaurus long neck and massive body were supported by its four strong limbs. Requiring such heavy bones to support it, Melanorosaurus’ physiology also included hollow spinal vertebrae to reduce its overall weight. An early sauropod, Melanorosaurus predated the even larger sauropods that dominated the Jurassic Period.

coloradisaurus.notes: Coloradisaurus is a genus of early sauropod dinosaurs. An omnivore dinosaur, it ate both meat and plants, which increased its chance for survival. Discovered in the Colorado mountain range of Argentina, this dinosaur’s naming gives us some insight into the scientific process of naming new discoveries: When it was discovered in 1978, it was originally named Coloradia, but this name had already been designated to a moth; so the name was changed. Adding to the naming lottery, Coloradisaurus is thought by some scientists to be an adult specimen of Mussaurus that was only discovered an infant and juvenile specimens.

diplodocus.attributes: 30 to over 100+ individuals in a single herd
diplodocus.notes: Diplodocus is one of the most recognizable dinosaurs, with a huge body, a long neck and tail, and strong limbs. For many years, it was considered to be the longest dinosaur, and is still one of the longest. So long, in fact, that its body design is often compared to modern day suspension bridges. Its size was often enough to deter Carnivorous predators such as Allosaurus and Ceratosaurus. Diplodocus name means “Double Beam” for its distinct bones in the underside of its tail.

spinosaurus.attributes: Crocodilian-like head, large sail on back
spinosaurus.notes: Larger than T. rex, Spinosaurus was the world’s largest carnivorous dinosaur, It name comes from the large fin on its back, which was probably a display feature. Spinosaurus hunted fish along the shore, and hunted smaller prey such as infant dinosaurs. The first Spinosaurus skeleton ever discovered and assembled by German scientists was destroyed during World War II in a night bombing raid. Recently, new specimens have been discovered in Egypt close to the location of the original discovery.

stegosaurus.attributes: Two pairs of pointed bony spikes at tail end
stegosaurus.notes: A large, heavily built, Herbivore quadruped, Stegosaurus had a distinctive and unusual posture and appearance. Its rounded back, short forelimbs, and head low to the ground allowed it lumber across the low areas of the American Southwest and Portugal as it grazes. Its stiffened spiked tail helped defend it against predators and its tall fins on its back assisted it in attracting mates and, possibly, in regulating body heat – acting almost like a cooling tower for its blood. Other relatives of Stegosaurus such as Kentrosaurus and Huayangosaurus have been identified in Asia and Europe. With a low brain to body ratio, Stegosaurus relied more on its brawn than its intelligence to survive. Perhaps it was more like the large loving family dog that was content to roam and eat – although whether it enjoyed belly rubs will likely never be known definitively.

coelophysis.notes: The creature before you is so much more than it appears. This is one of the first dinosaurs to roam the planet and it marks the beginning of the reign of the “Terrible Lizards” which is the meaning of the word dinosaur. This new species’ evolutionary advantage gave it a significant chance for success. Instead of being cold blooded (depending on outside temperatures to maintain body temperature, it could regulate its own body temperature (endothermic) which meant it could hunt both day and night. Being able to walk on its hind legs (bi-pedal), freed up its front limbs for grabbing at prey, which it could eat mercilessly with its large jaw and sharp teeth. This is one of the earliest dinosaurs and it changed the world, literally. And because it evolved before the great single landmass of Pangea broke up, its descendants spread all over the world without boats or airplanes!
